steps.en: What you see: The interventricular septum flattens and the left ventricle looks D shaped in short axis. The right atrium and right ventricle dilate and the free wall thickens. The tricuspid regurgitant velocity rises above 3.4 m per s in high probability disease. The pulmonary trunk dilates and the inferior vena cava engorges as right heart failure follows.

Normal values with units: Peak tricuspid regurgitant velocity. Normal 2.8 m per s or below. Intermediate 2.9 to 3.4 m per s. High probability above 3.4 m per s.. Source: ASE and EACVI 2016 diastolic function guideline, section on tricuspid regurgitant velocity

Systolic pulmonary pressure estimate. Four times velocity squared plus right atrial pressure. Below 36 mmHg low, 36 to 50 mmHg intermediate, above 50 mmHg high.. Source: ASE 2019 transthoracic examination guideline, section on Doppler and haemodynamics

Right atrial pressure from the vena cava. Cava 21 mm or below with 50 percent or more collapse suggests 5 mmHg. Dilated cava with below 50 percent collapse suggests around 15 mmHg.. Source: ASE 2019 transthoracic examination guideline, section on the inferior vena cava
Right ventricular basal diameter. Normal 42 mm or below in the focused view. Above this the ventricle is dilated.. Source: ASE 2019 transthoracic examination guideline, section on the right ventricle

ECG and heart sound correlation ecg: Right axis deviation with right ventricular hypertrophy marks pressure load. A tall R in lead V1 with a deep S in lead V6 completes the pattern. Peaked P waves mark right atrial enlargement.

ECG and heart sound correlation sounds: The pulmonary component of the second sound is loud. A pansystolic murmur marks functional tricuspid regurgitation. A right sided fourth sound with a palpable right ventricular heave marks a stiff failing ventricle.

What to report: Tricuspid velocity with the pressure estimate and the atrial pressure assumption stated
Septal shape in systole and diastole with right heart chamber sizes
Pulmonary trunk size, pulmonary regurgitation signal and any shunt
Left heart filling pressures to separate post capillary disease from pre capillary disease
Red flags needing urgent referral: Syncope with high probability disease, needs urgent pulmonary hypertension review
Right heart failure with liver congestion and ascites, needs urgent cardiology review
Suspected chronic clot disease with mismatched defects on imaging history, needs urgent thromboembolism workup
Pitfalls: Anaemia, fever and high output states raise velocity without vessel disease, so record haemoglobin and heart rate.
Severe free tricuspid regurgitation equalises pressures and underreads velocity, so integrate septal shape.
Left heart disease is the commonest cause of raised pressure, so grade diastolic function in every study.

todo.en: How to get it on the probe, step by step: Start in the short axis at papillary level and watch septal shape through systole and diastole.
Move to the focused right ventricle view and align continuous wave Doppler with the tricuspid jet.
Record the peak tricuspid velocity in m per s and add the right atrial pressure estimate.
Measure right atrial area, basal ventricular diameter and pulmonary trunk size.
Measure the inferior vena cava with sniff collapse for the atrial pressure estimate.
Common mistakes and how to correct them: Underreading tricuspid velocity with an off axis beam. Fix: Interrogate from several windows including the inflow view and keep the highest complete envelope.
Confusing pressure flattening with volume flattening. Fix: Systolic flattening means pressure overload while diastolic flattening means volume overload. Read each phase separately.
Calling every high velocity primary pulmonary hypertension. Fix: Treat lung disease, clots, sleep apnoea and left heart disease before labelling primary arterial disease.

remember.en: Separate pre capillary from post capillary patterns for referral.

q.en: Which tricuspid velocity marks high probability disease?

why.en: Above 3.4 m per s with systolic pressure above 50 mmHg marks high probability disease.

q.en: How is systolic pulmonary pressure estimated?

o.en: Four times velocity squared plus right atrial pressure

why.en: The Bernoulli equation converts velocity to gradient, then the atrial pressure estimate is added.

q.en: Systolic septal flattening is seen with a normal cava. What does it mean?

o.en: Volume overload flattens the septum in diastole

why.en: Systolic flattening marks pressure overload while diastolic flattening marks volume overload.

q.en: Syncope occurs with velocity 4.2 m per s and a dilated failing right ventricle. What next?

o.en: Start disease therapy on the echo alone
Urgent pulmonary hypertension review with cause workup

why.en: Syncope with high probability disease marks high risk and needs urgent specialist review with full cause workup.
